text:
maria: Heads up — tried capturing an nsys trace inside our k8s profiling job and the timeline is basically empty of CUDA kernels (we only get a few host-side syscalls). Running on GKE GPU nodes (driver 530, CUDA 11.8 runtime). Anyone seen this?

devin: yup. nsys inside an unprivileged container often can't talk to the NVIDIA device nodes / kernel tracing interfaces. Did you run the job with --gpus /device mounts only or with privileged/hostPID?

maria: We used the nvidia.com/gpu device and the standard runtime via nvidia-container-toolkit. No privileged, hostPID=false. Job YAML attached in the CI run.

devin: That explains it. nsys needs access to /dev/nvidia* and some kernel tracing hooks. Options (ordered by least friction -> most reliable):
- Run a short privileged DaemonSet on the node to capture from host namespace (recommended for reproducible traces).
- Start the container with hostPID: true and securityContext.privileged: true (quick but less safe).
- Mount device nodes manually: hostPath /dev/nvidia0,/dev/nvidiactl,/dev/nvidia-uvm and add CAP_SYS_ADMIN/CAP_SYS_PTRACE (sometimes required).

devin: Example sandbox job snippet we used locally:
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: nsys-capture
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      hostPID: true
      nodeSelector:
        cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-tesla-t4
      containers:
      - name: nsys
        image: nvcr.io/nvidia/nsight-systems:2023.4
        securityContext:
          privileged: true
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tmp
          mountPath: /tmp
      restartPolicy: Never
      volumes:
      - name: tmp
        emptyDir: {}
```

maria: Ok we'll try the DaemonSet approach. Any gotchas with nvidia-container-toolkit versions or driver/runtime mismatch?

sanjay: Yes — mismatch causes silent failures where you see driver talk but missing kernel samples. Also: if your workload launches many tiny kernels (KV cache lookups, small matmuls from batching heuristics), the timeline will be dominated by kernel launch overheads. In a perf trace we recently saw ~2000 kernel launches in 10s, each <10us, which looked cheap but added up due to launch latency.

sanjay: Perfetto/nsys timeline showed a pattern: big aten::matmul (fused) plus lots of small kernels for KV cache reads. Profiling in container hid the small kernels entirely — so we misattributed regression to batch scheduler.

oliver: If you can't run privileged, another path is node-level capture: ssh to node or use kubectl debug to start a privileged pod on the GPU node and run nsys from there. We used `kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=... --privileged` then ran the capture pointing to the container PID namespace.

maria: Good notes. Any quick analysis tips once we have a trace?

devin: Look at kernel timeline zoomed to microsecond scale. Filter by launch time and grouped names. If you see many tiny kernels with high inter-launch gaps, it's a launch-overhead problem. Check NVTX ranges from our runtime: see 'batch enqueue' vs 'kernel execute' tags. Also export the timeline CSV and run `awk` to bucket kernel durations (<10us, 10-100us, >100us).

sanjay: For KV cache specifically: ensure the cache lookup path is on-GPU (no host<->device roundtrips). If lookups are implemented as many 1-thread kernels, fuse them or move to a persistent kernel that handles a batch of lookups. Also consider increasing batch window to allow grouping of lookups into fewer kernels.

oliver: Another file-permission gotcha: nsys writes temporary capture files under /tmp or $HOME/.nsight-systems, which on k8s hostPath mounts can be owned by root and unreadable by the pod user. Make sure your hostPath or emptyDir mounts have correct mode or run with same UID.

maria: infra-bot spun up a quick privileged DaemonSet on gpu-node-pool for a 30s capture (job 173).

infra-bot: Created DaemonSet "nsys-capture-ds" targeting nodeSelector cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator=nvidia-tesla-t4. Logs will be uploaded to gs://redwood-profiles/1746056789/ .

devin: Once we have the trace, I'll look for kernel hotspot candidates (heavy matmul vs tiny kernels). If it's launch overhead, we can prototype a batching heuristic change: prefer slightly larger micro-batches (trade a few ms latency for much lower token-cost).

maria: Plan: 1) run node-level privileged capture (infra) 2) upload trace 3) sanjay/devin analyze for kernel launch pattern and KV cache hotspots 4) propose batching/kv fusion patch. Owners: infra=oliver, analysis=devin/sanjay, runtime PR=maria.

oliver: ping me when capture is done, I'll attach node-level logs (dmesg, /var/log/kern.log) in case driver messages show up.

maria: thanks all — will post trace link here when uploaded. :thumbsup:
